item.title: AIFP: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All
item.description:
METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario.

This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) before 2029. SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs.

Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report.

If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement. Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights (more).

Full post: https://blog.aifutures.org/p/q35-timelines-update-looks-like-the

item.title: What rogue agent swarms might look like
item.description:
TL;DR: Rogue agent swarms could soon become competent enough to multiply themselves and perform cyberattacks at levels never seen before. I present a dynamic simulation that estimates the expected size of these cyberattacks. With 2025-based estimates, it gives an average doubling time of 2.7 days for a rogue agent swarm. If the swarm grows unrestrained, it could cause trillions of dollars in damage in its first year.

#AI notice: This post is human-written. Opus 5.5 wrote the code for the simulation, suggested copyedits and supported research by finding relevant sources.

Introduction

Soon AI models might be skilled enough to form rogue agent swarms[1]. I believe it is important to think through what the competitive advantages of rogue swarms are, so we can put our defenses in the right places. For the purposes of this article a "rogue agent swarm" is really any system that can carry out cyberattacks for profit and runs fully digitally, allowing it to copy itself over and over[2]. This could be a single language model running for a long time. It can also be a group of different AI models, each only executing a small part[3].

The main advantage a rogue swarm could have is that it can put all of the gains from its criminal activity back into generating new copies of itself. Human criminal enterprises would instead take profits and have a hard time converting gains into more skilled labor.

The second competitive advantage I see for a rogue swarm is that it does not have to trace its money back to an original source. Human organizations, even illegal ones, will want to extract value from their enterprise. Taking that value out can leave traces and allow law officials to find the criminals and hold them accountable.
A rogue agent swarm never has to trace anything back to the original source. Any rogue agent that has enough resources/money to continue existing and possibly spawn a new agent could manage this without any contact with the rest of the swarm.

In general the agents run in one of two ways. Either they run open-source models on rented compute, or they call the APIs of big model providers to tap into their stronger capabilities. A clever rogue swarm would combine both to get an optimal trade-off between capabilities and the risk of getting caught.

In this post we will first cover the economics of a swarm and the basic idea of how it keeps replicating. Then we will look at how the simulation predicts a swarm will behave and what factors play a role. Next we will discuss its results and limitations. Finally we will turn to the recommendations that follow from them.

Economics

The first question is: how will rogue agents get more resources or make more money? An obvious solution is data blackmail. Data blackmail means that a hacker steals all of the data from some institution, such as a hospital, and then corrupts the original archives. The institution is then forced to choose between losing all of their data and giving in to the blackmail by paying. Data breaches are not the only way a swarm can make money, but they are the best studied. In Q3 2025 data extortion earned attackers $377k on average from each victim that paid[4]. Payouts vary a lot, and the total for 2025 was estimated at 900 million dollars[5].

If a single AI agent or small swarm pulled off one of these breaches, it could use the money to run more rounds of blackmail. The number of new rounds it could run is given by dividing the gain of one successful round of blackmail by the cost to produce it[6]. That ratio is the swarm's growth rate per generation. Once we know it, the next obvious question is: how long does one generation take?

Each generation has three steps: stealing the data, getting the victim to pay and spinning up new agents. In human-run organizations, stealing the data can be done in 3 days[7], but AI swarms could theoretically cut down on this time dramatically. There is one thing that is way less flexible: getting the victim to pay. Payment usually takes one or two weeks[8] for the victim to check their backups and to weigh whether paying is worth it for them. It is the one part of the loop that the attacker has the fewest options to shorten, so I expect that as swarms get more competent, payment time will be the main deciding factor in generation speed.

Model

We call the number of new attacks that one attack pays for the replication value, R. You might remember R from COVID estimates. It is calculated as follows. R is simply the gain per breach divided by the cost per breach. The gain per breach is then broken down into the ransom that is paid out in a successful attempt multiplied by some factors calculating the chance of success.

R = (share who pay × ransom × share kept after cashing out × share of agents not shut down) ÷ cost per breach

The simulation then uses R to calculate the ransom money gained every week and the number of targets that are left, which starts at 1 million by default, based on the 1.9 million companies with more than 100 staff and the 59% of mid-size organizations that get hit by ransomware in a year. If the agents do not know which targets they have already hit, about 1/R of the targets stay out of the swarm's reach in each attack cycle. If they are able to target only organizations they have not hit yet, they can exploit every available target.

Ransoms are spread over a range of sizes. The "Cost at 10x the ransom" bar represents how much more it costs to breach a target that pays a 10x bigger ransom. That value decides whether big or small targets are more profitable to attack. The agents are assumed to know which targets pay best, pick the low-hanging fruit first and only launch attacks with an individual R value above 1.

The simulation below estimates the growth rate of a rogue swarm. Every value is adjustable with the bars. Each bar has the values that cause the swarm to die out marked green. The top graph plots the income of the total replicating swarm each week and the bottom graph shows how many targets remain as each available target gets exploited. Push one of the bars into the green part and the swarm dies out.

Results

With 2025-based estimates and rough guesses[9] about the AI's skills, the default R value is 7.0 and the average doubling time is 2.7 days. The swarm would out-earn human gangs 25 days in and run out of targets on day 57. If the swarm runs out of targets, that means it has more funds than it can use for more breaches. By that point it has succeeded at a data breach on >80% of available targets in a period of two months. Compare this to the 1% of available targets that get breached per year today. That would be a catastrophic development: roughly $1.4T in damages over 840,000 organizations[10].

The simulation suggests that a self-replicating AI swarm taking off is overdetermined if it is possible at all. Once the first swarm exists, it would self-propagate in a wide range of possible worlds. We must make sure that swarms like this never form.

The process could already be underway, as AI models have proven capable of doing individual parts of the loop.[11] Next come the limitations of the simulation, followed by recommendations for potential targets, insurance companies, compute vendors and governments.

Limitations of this simulation

The simulation can be wrong in a couple of ways. First, it leaves out competition with human gangs and other swarms. Second, it ignores how defenders react. It only covers what happens by default if a single rogue swarm were deployed in an otherwise unprepared world.

Third, in the limit some of the assumptions break down. If the swarm has to launder billions of dollars per week, it will probably run into the limits of whatever channels it uses. In the same vein, other assumptions can change as effects of scale kick in.

Some assumptions favor the swarm. It can pick target sizes perfectly and its spawn time does not change with scale. Finally, the simulation assumes the swarm can buy compute without passing identity checks, though at high expense.

Other factors can change which values you would want to use. For example, the cost per breach will likely drop over time, and institutions will be less likely to pay an AI model with no track record of deleting data. Feed these changes into the simulation to see what needs to change for such a swarm not to be economically viable.

Recommendations

This is, to put it lightly, quite worrying. What can we do to prepare?

Several levers in the simulation can prevent the loop from forming. We should push on all of them if we want to be resistant to this kind of entity. That means shutting down rogue agents when they appear, setting up monitoring agencies to stop them from operating, making cashing out expensive and keeping ransoms low. Above all, the factor that I believe defenders have the most influence over is not paying the ransom.

Even if we push on only that one lever, we likely cannot push it far enough: at current averages, the payment rate would have to drop below 1% or over 95% of agents would have to be caught during operation. Each of these is an improbable goal on its own, but by working on all the levers at once we can cut the speed and effectiveness of any swarms that may come in the future.

Insurers need to set clear rules to stop reimbursing ransom payments. Crypto exchanges should build strong monitoring in advance. Cloud and API providers must watch for this behavior and stop it from spreading, and governments should enact payment bans and hold the other parties to their responsibilities. If it looks like a swarm has been created, the news must reach potential targets within a month, together with an industry-wide call to stop the agents from proliferating. Installing these monitors cannot wait until we see the first signs of these swarms. Once we see the first signs, a swarm like this is already on its way to causing catastrophic damage within weeks.

Finally, the AI companies building this dangerous technology should also be held accountable. We should make them liable for losses caused by misuse; after all, without their technology this destruction would not exist.


Author's note:
This post turned out a lot scarier than I had first anticipated. I might be wrong about some of the simulation's assumptions. I have done my best to capture the dynamics I expect to drive a swarm like this. I believe we are about to enter a time of turmoil in our digital spaces caused by Mythos-level hacking capabilities becoming available to open-weight models.

  1. ^

    In its August 2025 threat report, Anthropic describes one actor that used Claude Code to run data extortion against at least 17 organizations with ransom demands from $75k to $500k.

  2. ^

    METR's The Rogue Replication Threat Model talks about a similar scenario.

  3. ^

    A swarm could come about for many reasons. It could be explicitly set up by a criminal for a big ploy. But I think one will most likely form when someone asks an unaligned model to "Make Money" by any means necessary. For this post the swarm's end goal does not matter, only how it behaves.

  4. ^

    SecurityWeek

  5. ^

    The Record reported that Chainalysis tracked around $820M in on-chain ransomware payments over 2025 and it expects the total to exceed $900M as more data comes in.

  6. ^

    The formula used is R = (share who pay × ransom × share kept after cashing out × share of agents not shut down) ÷ cost per breach

  7. ^

    Sophos found in their 2025 Active Adversary Report that it takes a median of about 3 days from the start of an attack to data exfiltration.

  8. ^

  9. ^

  11. ^

This is about 2,000x below the roughly $100k per breach above which this swarm can no longer proliferate.

item.title: How to Preserve Critical Thinking in the Age of Agents
item.description:
In a world where much of the Systems-2 thinking is done by agents, I find myself more and more going towards cognitive atrophy. Even in my daily work, most of my tasks are superbly executed by autonomous agents while I sit there staring at my screen. The dopamine rush that I used to get while once solving a bug, writing significant code, or thinking something from first principles is fading.

Eventually I might lose this ability forever, and hence one fine day I thought to myself to make a list of all the things (activities/skills whatever you may say) I can do to get that control back. This by no means is exhaustive; however, I have tried to cover a wide variety spanning mathematics, logical thinking, programming, and problem solving in general.
Please feel free to suggest more in the comments.

Here's the list.

  1. Try making forcasts about actual real events. Assign them probabilities, write down your reasoning, and revisit them when the outcomes are known. See Metaculus
  2. Solve a puzzle hunt where you must first figure out the rules of each puzzle. See MIT Mystery Hunt Archive
  3. One of my favorites is to try to decipher an unfamiliar language with examples. Work out its grammar and translate sentences you have never seen. Try International Linguistics Olympiad problems
  4. Building a defensible model from incomplete information and trying to estimate something that almost seems impossible to know exactly. Talking about Fermi Estimation here.
  5. If you love coding, try competitive programming. (SPOJ and CSES are good places to start.)
  6. If you love mathematics, start solving olympiad problems (start here)
  7. If you really love mathematics, you should try writing detailed proofs of mathematical theorems from first principles. If you’re new to proof-writing, start with Book of Proof. For an extra challenge, try formalizing your proofs using Lean.
  8. If you love coding & mathematics, try solving Project Euler
  9. Learn a card game that requires reasoning about hidden information, such as bridge
  10. Solve problems from IMO or IPhO or IChO or IOAA (pick your favorite subject)
  11. For ML coding enthusiasts—Use DeepML
  12. Take philosophical questions from the International Philosophy Olympiad and ponder over them—write down your essays and revisit them from time to time. (imho—essay writing opens your mind)
  13. If you feel the above is too hard - Check out the general questions from Oxford's All Soul Exam
  14. Reproduce a published figure, then change an assumption and see if the conclusion still holds up or not. Johns Hopkins Open Case Studies has examples.
  15. Read any scientific paper (according to your domain of expertise) and design an experiment that could show its main claim as incorrect
  16. Keep a notebook of questions you cannot answer. Every week, choose one and investigate it from first principles. Try to reason using Bayesianism
  17. Make your own fantasy world!
  18. Read "The Art of Language Invention" and make your own language
  19. Choose a decision made by a historical figure. List the information available to them at the time, then defend or criticize the decision without using hindsight.
  20. Edit a paragraph until it is half its original length without losing its meaning. (Without an AI of course!)
  21. Try to cook a dish without a recipe. Form a hypothesis about one change, test it, and record the result.
  22. Learn physical skills like juggling, cardistry, and calligraphy

item.title: Which state AGs are ready to be proactive on AI?
item.description:
If federal action in the US isn't forthcoming on AI, state Attorneys General (AGs) may end up being a central force on regulation of AI. I tasked Opus 5.5 with helping me collect some data on the actions that the various state AGs have taken on AI, to try to understand how much appetite there is among the states to take on AI companies.

Summary

  • Every state office has sent some kind of signal that they are willing to take on AI companies (e.g. signing a letter to an AI company)
  • A smaller group of states (15) have taken at least 1 step that indicates willingness to take initiative or lead actions against AI companies (e.g. opening its own investigation)
  • Several states in the second group (4) may now be in flux with a new Attorney General coming into office after the 2026 midterms
  • Only two states have an AG who has led or acted alone on AI and has a 1 GW or more data center within the state

The state of state AGs

With the help of Opus 5.5, I collected data from the websites of state AGs on the various actions that each state has been involved in. I have Opus classify the actions each state is involved in and use these assignments to place the states into tiers 1-4, with higher tiers indicating that a state has taken more aggressive action to regulate AI. I think the move from 2 to 3 is particularly interesting, since this reflects the difference between a state passively joining actions by other AGs and an office initiating or leading actions itself. You can see the results of coding the states in this way below:

Most states have at least joined a brief, investigation or suit, although for many states the only action putting them in this category is the Character.AI bankruptcy. Some state-specific observations:

  • NY is only at a 2 despite having a dedicated tech unit in the office and having some state-level appetite to regulate AI with the RAISE Act.
  • NM is at a 1 despite the AG there having just won a large jury verdict against Meta over data privacy violations.
  • TX is at a 4, and has a track record of taking tech cases through multiple appeals as well as several large settlements with Meta and Google. However, Texas will have a new AG coming in after the midterms, and the state's courts may also be in flux with changes on its 15th Court of Appeals, which hears appeals from its new business court.
  • With TX being something of a question mark and now having an incoming Democratic AG, FL may be the state to take up leadership on tech issues among Republican states. The FL AG is currently pursuing a high-profile investigation/lawsuit against OpenAI, suggesting a strong appetite for action on AI.

Data Centers

In my data, only 2 of the tier 3/4 states also have a 1GW+ data center located in the state (TX and KY). Having a data center in the state could create economic incentives that make an AG more hesitant to oppose AI companies (which is potentially consistent with many of the data center states joining instead of leading). On the other hand, I could imagine having a data center in the state being an important jurisdictional hook, particularly in scenarios where AI capabilities accelerate rapidly and states become interested in getting a lot more aggressive on regulation. Consider a situation like the one in AI2040, where accelerating AI capabilities are rapidly changing the world and AI is a central political issue. In the absence of federal action, a coalition of states might try to implement a local version of plan S or A (i.e. stopping or significantly slowing AI development using levers within those states). AI companies seeking to continue developing ever more advanced models might attempt to get around these limitations by leaving the jurisdiction of those states. Having an AI data center located in-state would be one of the strongest limiting factors for this kind of scenario, since an AI company that is physically training or running their models on a data center in a state would almost certainly be subject to that state's jurisdiction.

Limitations

I may have coded some actions incorrectly or missed some actions that an AG has been involved in. Please feel free to comment below or reach out to me with corrections or actions I may have missed.

item.title: Day 1 Pre-Notes—Strategy Course (August 2026 Version)
item.description:
Written for the August 2026 version of the course (ie. the previous version)

These unofficial notes were written for a previous version of the BlueDot strategy course (last run August 2026). They “pre-notes” in that they are intended to be shared before the session. They aim to supplement the readings; I have made no attempt to summarise them. I always emphasise to students that this is bonus material, rather than core. As supplementary material, these notes are targeted at a much higher context audience than the course itself.

Since this course is no longer being actively run, I'm prioritising getting these notes out there over perfect copy editing. I have some additional notes on the different actors that were listed in the old exercise which I will be publishing soon.

Preparing for Launch:

  • “The benefits of AI progress may not come quickly enough… For example, markets alone may not prioritize AI that automates the replication of scientific studies, or investigate new medical treatments that can’t be patented, or conduct basic research in neuroscience with no immediate commercial applications” — to what extent is this research dual-use? Insofar as it is dual use, are there ways of accessing these capabilities that don’t produce these externalities? Conversely, will these efforts have a significant impact or are separate efforts unnecessary given how rapidly AI has developed anyway:
    • Currently, AI is rapidly accelerating our progress in maths research and now we’re starting to see results in physics. Should we expect to see similar progress in other scientific fields as well soon, or will these domains prove much less tractable?
    • Deepmind dismantled its Nobel-Prize Winning AlphaFold Team. Is this an indicator that Google believes domain-specific work is unnecessary or is this purely a commercial decision driven by Gemini falling behind?
  • “AI safety researchers have devoted insufficient attention to solutions that assume that dangerous AI capabilities will rapidly diffuse”:
    • The difference here may be overstated: most AIS folk believe that capabilities will rapidly diffuse and simply want to intervene to make it less rapid on the margin (that said, some folks are optimistic that compute governance might enable longer-term pauses).
    • Helen Toner has argued that Nonproliferation is the wrong approach to AI misuse (she allows for narrow, time-bound exceptions). She is worried that preventing diffusion will become harder and harder over time; and that doing so will require increasing invasive methods. The main argument on the other side is that there will likely be at least one attack vector where offence-defence balance will significantly favours the attacker (see Problems of Proliferation),
    • It’s worth noting that it’s possible that both could be true (ie. proliferation being almost impossible to stop AND the offence-defence balance massively favouring the attacker). I mention this because I’ve often seen people to talk past each other by focusing on why their point means that the other side’s solution won’t work without acknowledging that the other side also thinks they have identified a similarly strong weakness. In these kinds of situations, it’s very common for both sides to just repeat their point again, but louder. Whilst this can implicitly communicate “I think my point is the most relevant consideration”; it is almost never persuasive.
  • Leveraging the “jagged frontier”: These kinds of approaches have gained a lot more attention in the AI safety community recently (see, for example, AI Tools for Existential Security or ‘AI for societal uplift’ as a path to victory). Back in the day, most people in the AI safety community expected a fast takeoff, so people were more pessimistic about utilising AI as part of a sociotechnical approach to making AI go well (instead people tended to focus more on the question of whether we ask AI to solve the alignment problem for us).
  • “Closely tracking the frontier of AI capabilities in different domains could give us the advanced warning necessary to proactively build new defenses”:
    • Lawrence Chan’s claims that: We’re actually running out of benchmarks to upper bound AI capabilities. Automated evaluations may provide a way to keep pace, but what if this strategy doesn’t prove viable?
    • How well did society prepare for Mythos-level cyber capabilities and autonomous swarms? Prima facie, it certainly looks like society didn’t adequately prepare, but insofar as teams take a defense-in-depth approach and learn from each other, it’s possible that these system will prove more resilient than you might think.
    • If you think society is underprepared, then this provides a prima facie case for being more pessimistic about resilience measures for other AI risks too, on the other hand, if you think it’s overblown, then you might be less worried.
  • This article suggests that we should hold a “fairly deep uncertainty” to risks from AI.
    • If there is substantial uncertainty, how should we handle it? Does the burden of proof lie on those who claim models are dangerous or those who claim that these risks are manageable?
    • In constrast to Preparing for Launch, MIRI argues that some predictions about the future are “hard calls” and others are “easy calls”: “But some facts about the future are predictable. If you, personally, buy a lottery ticket tomorrow, we don’t know what complicated theories or whims you’ll use to pick your numbers, and we don’t know what numbers will come up, but all that uncertainty adds up to a very strong prediction that you will not win the lottery. Similarly, if you drop an ice cube into a glass of hot water, it’s impossibly complicated to predict where each molecule will end up ten minutes later—but all that uncertainty adds up to a near-certain prediction that the ice cube will melt. Half of physics is like that: We can’t calculate which exact path gets taken, but we know where almost all paths lead.... Successful forecasting...is about finding aspects of the future that become easy calls when viewed from the right angle.” (indirectly source)
    • As such, MIRI believes that we can be fairly confident that attempting to build a superintelligence with current techniques would kill us, but that it’s silly to try to predict exactly how it would kill us. Are they correct that most people are too ready to throw up their hands and say, “there’s so much uncertainty, who could possibly know?” instead of trying to work out which questions we can or can’t answer?

Seeking Stability in the Competition for AI Advantage:

  • One potential criticism against MAIM is that rather than merely describing the default state, the authors are actually hyperstitioning it into reality (intentionally or unintentionally). Proponents of MAIM would argue that Hegseth attempting to declare Anthropic a supply chain risk demonstrates that as AI increased in power, it was always going to be increasingly securitized. On the other hand, some people might feel that this is reading too much into this (for example, a lot of how things played out seems like it is contingent on the happenstance of Hegseth being defence secretary).
    • See Mutual Sabotage of AI Probably Won’t Work for a second critique.
  • In Situational Awareness, Leopold argues that given the national security implications, a Manhattan project for AI (“The Project”) is inevitable. He list some merits of The Project, but he emphasises that it’ll happen regardless of what we do, so we just have to make the best of it. This is covered in Day 4, but if you want a preview, check out this Youtube short.
  • In constrast, Convergence Analysis argues that full nationalisation is unlikely. They observe that US policymakers generally endorse free-market competition, “practical, legal and political challenges” and the ability for the government to achieve its goals via less coercive means. They argues that “soft” nationalisation is more likely and they then lay out a number of such mechanisms that would constitute different levels of intervention (just to be clear, they aren’t advocating for soft-nationalism, just predicting it). Here’s a diagram showing their measure for one particular category:
  • Proponents of such a view would point to recent actions of the Trump administration as vindication.

It’s practically impossible to run a big AI company ethically:

  • It’s worth noting that Anthropic has updated its policy positions since then in Policy on the AI Exponential. They argue the advancing capabilities require the following action: “This calls for government action and for regulation—regulations that are carefully designed to prevent government overreach and protect innovation. When a model poses risks of this kind, the government should have the legal authority to block or deter its deployment—beyond what exists in current law or in existing proposals in Congress—with civil penalties tied to global annual revenue that escalate with repeated violations. Frontier AI developers should have to test these models, be transparent to the public about their findings, submit them to independent evaluation, and maintain a robust security program.”:
    • Even more recently, the leading labs incl. Anthropic agree to the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, which proposes to four layers of verification for safety.
  • On the topic of funding, Anthropic ended up copying OpenAI and accepting Gulf State investments. Dario defended his decision: “Unfortunately, I think ‘No bad person should ever benefit from our success’ is a pretty difficult principle to run a business on”. Training frontier models is very expensive, so it’s hard for the labs to be picky.

(This chart is unfortunately older than I’d like; published June 2024).

In search of a dynamist vision for safe superhuman AI:

  • Honestly, I wish this reading were later in the course, as I think it is somewhat less useful in the first week of a course where many people may be new to these debates. For example, I see push back against the Vulnerable World Hypothesis as useful if you already know what it is and why it might be true. On the other hand, if you’re told that something you have never heard of before could actually be false, it is much less useful and much harder to evaluate her claims yourself (as opposed to just taking her word for it). Similarly, whilst the article’s rather terse criticisms of some common perspectives in the space, is useful pushback for folks debately enmeshed inside these debates (I agree with Paul Graham that merely contradicting someone often has value, as it pushes you to think about whether you are actually confident in your assertion), it’s not the ideal form of communication with folks who might only have a vague idea of the views she is criticising:
    • I would suggest that the recent results from AI in maths and physics cut against her argument insofar as they suggest that innovation may be the default. I would further suggest that the AI safety community has actually been driving a lot of the current dynamism. I think part of her argument survives—if only a few companies train frontier models then there is the threat of a ‘monoculture’ or at least a cultural oligarchy—but I suspect this is best analysed more concretely. Similarly, if AI enabled the rise of more despotic or totalitarian governments, that would be the complete opposite of her vision, but again, I suspect more concrete analysis would be more persuasive.
    • I certainly wouldn’t want to completely rule out there being a place for this kind of very high level abstract analysis, but even so, I would like to see this start by grounding itself in how we should address concrete problems posed by AI and then expand out from there. I think her article offers a useful frame, but I suspect that this is what taking these ideas further would look like.
    • Aren’t my notes subject to the same criticism of not being well suited as a first introduction to AI safety? Yes, but as supplementary material I’m intentionally targeting them at a higher level. This improves the ability of the course to serve those who might otherwise find it a bit too introductory.
  • I want to say a few words in defense of Nick Bostrom’s paper. Let’s suppose you’re thinking seriously about what technologies we might invent in the future. We live in a world where nukes exist, so it’s clearly possible to invent technologies that are extremely destructive and which are pretty hard to defend against. I would be surprised if nukes were literally the worst such technology. So this quickly leads to the following questions: “Are there some technologies where it would be better if they didn’t exist?” and “Is it possible to invent something so dangerous that we might have to rethink civil liberties?“. Arriving at these questions is a sign that you’re thinking seriously about the future, but, of course, merely asking the question doesn’t force you to answer one way or another. Whilst for some people, it feels obvious that if such a “black ball” technology was invented, we ought to be willing to take extreme measures to defend ourselves, there are many people on the complete opposite end, who resonate much more with “live free or die”.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.

item.title: Need for Speed
item.description:
In previous posts I argued that we will soon have a lot of AI workers. Here we look at how fast each of them will be. There is a big difference between a million AI workers plodding along at human speed and "only" ten thousand that each work a hundred times faster.

In short, today's AIs perform the tasks they can do about ten times faster than humans. At the point they can do human work in general, I expect individual copies would work at closer to human speed, though they would still finish long tasks considerably faster by working around the clock and splitting work across copies. Suitable hardware could raise their raw speed to perhaps a thousand times that of humans.

How fast do AIs run today?

Language models produce text by sequentially generating tokens, each corresponding to about three-quarters of a word. Here is how fast providers read and write tokens for a single user, as measured by Artificial Analysis in October 2026:

Most models write around 50 to 300 tokens per second whatever their size and read inputs fifty to a hundred times faster, as estimated from the time to the first output token. Reading is much faster than writing because models can process all of their input tokens in parallel, but must generate output tokens one after another. We discuss how tokens are generated in more detail in Appendix A.

Token speed is the most straightforward measure of how fast a language model runs, but it says little about how much work the model gets done. Small models like Haiku or Luna produce tokens much faster than beefy ones like Astra or Fable, but each token is worth less. For this reason, I'm skeptical of naive comparisons of AI and human speed that equate token for "token" (whatever that means for humans). A small model can produce vast quantities of AI slop far more quickly than a human can write, but that is no more interesting than observing that a program spitting words out at random can generate "text" billions of times faster than a human.

A more useful approach is to compare how fast humans and AIs do the same tasks. In my previous post, I found that when AIs can do human work, they need on the order of floating-point operations (FLOP) per second of human time replaced. This number varies a lot with the task and the model, and the estimates behind it are very noisy, but it is consistent across a broad range of tasks, spanning many domains and time horizons.

Dividing a model's FLOP per second by this number gives its speed relative to a human. Frontier models compute at around FLOP per second while writing (as can be seen from the grey diagonals in the above plot) and so typically perform output-heavy tasks about ten times faster than humans, ignoring gains from parallelizing work across agents. Those same models read tokens at above FLOP per second, and so on reading-heavy tasks can perform hundreds of times faster than humans.

In my post on AI compute, I estimated that if we develop AI systems capable of doing human work in the near future, they will require to FLOP per second of human time; this is somewhat higher than existing tasks, because mean costs are dominated by those tasks that are relatively expensive. As we discuss in Appendix A, such models would probably run at a similar number of FLOP per second as today's models, since these speeds are set by the hardware they run on. They would therefore perform output-heavy work at roughly human speed, while reading inputs a hundred times faster than humans.

Despite not being much faster than humans at writing, these AIs would still work much faster overall. Reading is a substantial fraction of most jobs, so reading a hundred times faster could roughly double their speed, and working around the clock rather than a 40-hour week gives another factor of about four. Together these would make AI workers about ten times faster than humans.

Probably the most important effect, though, is that AI systems can split work across many copies. You may have already witnessed this if you've used Claude Code recently to ask a seemingly straightforward question only to discover, half an hour and several hundred dollars later, that Claude had set up fifty subagents to meticulously investigate each individual proposed Iberian–Basque cognate. In principle, humans could also divide work in this way, but coordination overheads, like the fact you cannot easily hire 100 contractors and then fire them an hour later, make this impractical. On tasks that allow suitable parallelism, AIs could act hundreds of times faster than humans can.

Speed vs utilization

Providers charge more for faster services. OpenAI normally serves GPT-6.1 Sol at around 80 tokens per second, but offers services two and four times faster for twice and six times the price. Anthropic likewise charges twice as much for a fast mode of Claude Opus 5.5 that it says writes up to 2.5 times faster.

These speedups are possible because providers can trade off their hardware utilization, the fraction of the time their GPUs spend doing arithmetic, against speed per user by changing how they batch users and distribute them over GPUs. Batching lets you serve more users at once, which increases utilization but slows down each user. Splitting a model across many GPUs serves each user faster, but the GPUs then spend more time communicating with each other. We discuss how this works in Appendix A.

Typical tradeoffs between utilization and speed per user look something like this:

The dashed line shows the simple model we develop in Appendix A for Llama 3.1 70B. The other curves show the model of Erdil (2025) for models served on H100s, which includes more architectural detail and also speculative decoding, a method that lets a model generate several tokens per pass and in practice makes it about two times faster.

Judging by prices and published statistics, providers usually serve models in the middle of these curves, trading off utilization and speed roughly evenly. DeepSeek's serving statistics imply a utilization of around 10%.

Suppose you have a fixed number of chips. How fast should you run your AIs? The chips' total output, in tokens per second, is proportional to their utilization , and each AI running at speed takes of it, so the number of AIs you can run is

As a simple model, suppose the rate at which they get work done on a project is

where captures the diminishing returns to adding more AIs. For Llama 3.1 70B on H100s, using Erdil's utilization curve, the rate of work at each speed is:

If the work parallelizes well, with near one, it is best to run AIs slowly to maximize utilization, but for serial work with near zero, it is best to run them as fast as possible.

How fast could future AIs run?

Today's speeds are set by GPUs, which are designed to serve many users cheaply rather than one user fast. Even at almost zero utilization, they serve large models at no more than a few hundred tokens per second. Hardware built for speed could be much faster.

In Appendix B, we estimate how quickly models could be served on hardware optimized for speed. Even with heavy optimization, a number of steps must happen in sequence in each layer of the model, and the time these take is set by the hardware's clock speed, which is in turn limited by the physics of silicon transistors.

At today's clock speeds, on hardware that is otherwise optimistically designed but not wired around a particular model, we estimate these steps take at least about 1 µs per layer, suggesting maximum speeds of

where is the number of layers, is the time per layer, and is the number of active parameters. Even allowing higher clock speeds or hardware wired around a single model, I think going much faster than this is probably not feasible.

Hardware that could run models approaching these speeds doesn't exist today, and designing it would take substantial engineering. But, as we discuss at the end of Appendix B, tokens served on it would probably cost several times more than on GPUs, not orders of magnitude more.

If human-level AI requires a model with roughly a trillion active parameters and a hundred layers, and to FLOP per second to match a human, then on such hardware it would perform tasks a few hundred to a few thousand times faster than a human could. Getting beyond this with faster hardware seems very hard.

Alternatively, models might match human performance with substantially fewer FLOP. For this to make them much faster at fixed depth, they would have to produce fewer tokens per second of human work replaced. Working at ten thousand times human speed, for example, would mean matching each second of human work with a single token, assuming the depth remains at a hundred layers. When humans are typing or speaking, they produce about a token per second, so replicating that work with fewer tokens seems quite difficult.

Decreasing model depth could also increase speed, but the room for this is limited. The model we assumed is already only about a hundred layers deep, and some depth is presumably needed to do the relevant calculations. Perhaps a looped architecture, which uses calculations from previous tokens more extensively, could reduce the depth needed somewhat further.

These speeds stack with the advantages from the first section. Reading faster and working around the clock add roughly another factor of ten, and parallelism more on tasks that can be split up. On the right hardware, AIs could do human work thousands to tens of thousands of times faster than people.

Appendix A: How tokens are generated

In this appendix, we develop a simple model of how fast a language model generates tokens on GPUs. We ignore the additional complications that come from the KV cache, mixture-of-experts routing, and other architectural details. The interested reader can find a more detailed treatment in Erdil (2025) or Reiner Pope's conversation with Dwarkesh Patel.

Outputs from a single GPU

Start with the simplest case, a model with parameters running on a single GPU. Suppose that each parameter is stored in one byte, so that the weights take up bytes, and that they fit in the GPU's memory. Each pass requires the GPU to do two things. First, it must read every weight out of its memory and onto the chip where the arithmetic happens, which takes a time

Each token needs FLOP, so the compute performed for each user is

whatever the size of the model. A larger model produces fewer tokens per second, but does proportionately more arithmetic for each one.

The batch size trades speed against efficiency. A natural measure of efficiency is the utilization, the fraction of each step the GPU spends on arithmetic,

Below , each additional user raises the utilization without slowing anyone down. Above , the GPU is fully used and its output is fixed by the arithmetic, so each additional user just slows everyone down. The best operating point is thus around .

One additional effect is that every layer comes with fixed delays that do not depend on how much data is processed. Each step of the layer has to be started, intermediate results pass through the GPU's memory, and the GPU's processors have to synchronize before the next step can begin. Inputs from a single GPU

Before writing anything, the model has to read its input. Each input token has its own vector at every layer, so it needs one multiplication and one addition per weight, just like an output token. Unlike output tokens, though, input tokens are all known in advance, so the GPU can pass all of them through each layer together, using each weight it reads for every one of them. Reading the input therefore works exactly like serving a batch of users, and takes at least time

For inputs longer than tokens the process is compute-bound:

thus a single user's input is read times faster than its output is written. In practice the ratio is lower, mainly because measured reading speeds include fixed delays before the first token, and speculative decoding speeds up writing but not reading.

Outputs from multiple GPUs

Now suppose we have multiple GPUs and want to split the calculations among them. This introduces a third time-consuming process, that of transferring data between GPUs. Each transfer takes a time

where is a fixed delay, is the length of each user's vector (assuming two bytes per number), and is the bandwidth of the link between GPUs, in bytes per second. With typical values,

where the reference values are a typical fixed delay, the vector length of Llama 3.1 70B, and the link between H100s in the same server.

The naive way to split the calculations among GPUs is to give each one of the model's layers. Each layer needs the output of the one before, so the GPUs work in turn, with transfers per token:

This does not speed anything up. In fact, the additional transfers slightly slow each token down. Nor does it increase utilization. Splitting a model this way only makes sense when its parameters do not fit on a single GPU.

Instead, the GPUs can make each token much faster by sharing the work within each layer, with each GPU holding a slice of every layer's weights. Each GPU then computes a partial result for the whole batch, and the GPUs have to add these up about twice per layer (Shoeybi et al. (2019)), so each token needs exchanges.

An exchange takes two rounds. The batch's vectors are split into pieces, one owned by each GPU. In the first round, each GPU sends every piece to its owner, which adds them up. In the second, each owner sends its finished piece to all the other GPUs. All the GPUs send at the same time, and in each round each one sends and receives of the batch's bytes, so

where and are the fixed delay and the bandwidth with which each GPU can send to the other .

GPUs are typically wired together in groups of , 8 in an H100 server and 72 in a GB200 NVL72 rack. Within a group, the GPUs share a fast switch, so for the fixed delay and bandwidth are those of the transfers above, about 5 µs and 450 GB/s on H100s, whatever is. An exchange then takes about two transfers however many GPUs share the work. Once is larger than , some of the GPUs are connected by network links, which on an H100 server carry 50 GB/s per GPU, about an order of magnitude less, and have longer fixed delays. Exchanges therefore slow down sharply as soon as they cross between groups, and only gradually after that as more groups are added (Erdil (2025)).

A provider chooses and . Increasing the number of GPUs makes each user faster, but decreases utilization, as the GPUs must wait for exchanges at each step. Increasing the number of users increases utilization, but slows everyone down, through both the arithmetic and the larger exchanges. Appendix B: How fast can you go?

With enough chips, all the work that can be done in parallel takes no time, and the speed of a model is set by the steps that must happen in sequence. Each token passes through layers in turn. Within each layer, arithmetic operations must happen in sequence, and partial results computed in different places must be gathered together times. Each of these steps takes some number of clock cycles, so the time per token is

where is the duration of one clock cycle, is the number of cycles one arithmetic operation takes, and is the number of cycles one gathering takes, whether between parts of one chip or between chips.

Clock speed

Modern GPUs run at about 2 GHz, so ns, and the clock speeds of microprocessors have barely risen since the mid-2000s:

Clock speeds stalled in the mid-2000s because chips reached the limit of how much heat they could shed. A faster clock not only means more switches per second, but also higher voltages and as a result power consumption grows with the cube of the clock speed. Small increases in speed therefore create much greater cooling requirements, and even beyond this maximum voltages are limited because the thin insulating layers in transistors would wear out quickly. Even someone willing to pay much higher power costs would have difficulty achieving clock speeds much beyond 10 GHz without switching to fundamentally different physics.

Arithmetic

Each matrix multiplication ends with sums of thousands of numbers, and adding numbers in pairs takes steps however many chips are available. A layer of Llama 3.1 70B has vectors of numbers and contains nine such sums in sequence, which together with about ten other operations make . The exact number varies with architectural choices, and some of these steps can be done in parallel, but I think for any realistic architecture.

On a GPU, an arithmetic operation takes about four clock cycles, so , and the total arithmetic takes about 500 cycles, or 0.2 µs, per layer. But there are faster ways to do the required arithmetic. For instance, summing each digit position of a long series of numbers separately cuts the clock cycles needed for each sum about tenfold. With such tricks, the average operation takes about one clock cycle, so and the arithmetic in a layer takes roughly 100 clock cycles, or about 50 ns.

Gathering

A layer's weights are spread across a large area of silicon, and each multiplication happens next to the weight it uses. Each number a layer produces is a sum of thousands of these products, so before the next step can start, the products must be brought to one place and added, and the result sent back out to wherever the next weights are. Some of these sums can happen at the same time, so the number of gatherings that must happen in sequence depends on the architecture and on how the work is laid out. For Llama 3.1 70B on typical hardware, is roughly six.

On GPUs, a gathering takes a couple of microseconds, several thousand clock cycles, with software optimized for speed, whether within one GPU (Hazy Research) or between GPUs in a server (Shen et al. (2026)). With standard software, a gathering between GPUs takes closer to 10 µs, so the two in each layer add about 20 µs to the 60 µs fixed delay within each GPU that we used in Appendix A. GPU processors pass numbers to one another through memory shared across the whole chip, and each trip to that memory takes hundreds of clock cycles, which is why gatherings are slow for these chips.

A faster approach is to directly send each message to where it is needed. On chips designed for speed, messages move in short hops between neighboring parts of the chip, with each hop taking at least one clock cycle, and routing a message takes additional cycles. Such chips, like the Groq's AI chips or D. E. Shaw Research's Anton 3, need roughly 50 to 150 clock cycles, around 50 ns, to gather results across one chip (Abts et al. (2020); Shim et al. (2022)), so within one chip.

Each layer of a frontier model is usually too big to fit on one chip, and so gatherings require communication between chips. This is slow because signals leaving a chip's package must pass through a limited number of connections and travel over long, noisy paths, so each connection runs at very high speed through circuits that take tens of nanoseconds to send and decode a message. Crossing between chips takes 55 ns on Anton 3 and 300 ns on Groq's chips (Bitar et al. (2026)), so a gathering that must cross between chips and back takes several hundred cycles or more. For frontier models we therefore assume about 300 cycles per gathering, roughly Anton 3's crossing between chips and back plus a gathering within each chip.

The only fundamental limit on gathering is the time it takes a signal to cross the hardware holding a layer. Light travels 30 cm every nanosecond, but signals on a chip typically move ten or more times slower, so a layer spread over several centimeters of silicon requires at least a few nanoseconds for each gathering.

In principle, hardware could get close to this by wiring each gathering to follow the model's structure, so that results travel on dedicated wires rather than in hops, and by keeping each layer on a single wafer or package, so that no gathering crosses a slow link between chips. Such hardware could cut a gathering to tens of cycles, but would only perform well for limited model architectures.

Overall speed

Putting the terms together, we estimate that a layer on hardware optimized for latency would take

which gives an approximate, optimistic answer of about 1 µs. This is dominated by gathering rather than by arithmetic.

For comparison, the fastest hardware so far is a chip from Taalas, which takes about 2 µs per layer, but for a model small enough to fit on a single chip, Llama 3.1 8B, with its weights printed directly into the chip's wiring. Cerebras, which builds each chip from a whole silicon wafer, took 17 µs per layer for the same model at its launch, and the fastest GPU runs take about 50 µs.

At what cost?

How much more would it cost to run a model near this maximum speed? Hardware built for it would differ from a GPU in two main ways.

First, its memory. One way to supply the weights fast enough would be to store them in SRAM, the fast memory built into a chip, which costs about ten times as much per byte as the HBM that GPUs use, roughly $100 per GB for TSMC's densest SRAM at $30,000 per wafer against about $12 for HBM.

This need not raise the cost per token though, because the memory is shared by everyone a copy of the model serves. A fast copy could pipeline users through its layers, so that a hundred-layer model serves a hundred users at 10,000 tokens per second each, about a million tokens per second. A GPU copy of any sufficiently large model produces at most about 10,000 tokens per second, so the hundredfold higher output more than offsets the tenfold higher memory price.

Second, its arithmetic. Each token needs the same arithmetic however fast it is produced. In a simple design that processes one token at a time in each layer, arithmetic sized to finish in a few tens of nanoseconds would sit idle about 95% of the time, waiting for gathering. The hardware could instead carry much less arithmetic, taking about as long as the gathering, which would keep it busy about half the time at the cost of roughly halving the speed.

Keeping the arithmetic busy also requires every layer to be working at once, since each layer's arithmetic sits on its own chips. This requires pipelining, with a different user in each layer at any moment. Because each user's data also spends time in transit between layers, filling the pipeline takes somewhat more users than there are layers, and it loses efficiency whenever there are too few users or their traffic is uneven.

The memory and arithmetic of hardware built for speed therefore need not cost much more per token than a GPU's, provided it can be pipelined efficiently. Its networks and packaging would have to meet much tighter latency requirements, which could make them more expensive, though I don't know how much. My guess is that tokens served this way would cost several times more than on GPUs, but not orders of magnitude more.

Nobody yet knows how to build such chips, so at present they cannot be bought at any price, and substantial R&D would be needed to create them. The more closely they are tailored to a particular model architecture, the faster they can be and the fewer models they can run. Our estimate assumes chips heavily tailored to the kind of models in use today, but not to a single architecture. In the extreme, the weights can be printed into the chip, as Taalas does, so that each chip runs a single model. The more specialized the chip, the fewer chips its R&D is spread over, and the more value it loses when the models it was built for become obsolete.
